invective

in-VEK-tiv · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Invective is abusive or highly critical language.

The critic's review wasn't just negative -- it was pure invective, tearing apart every choice the director had made.

Worked Example

The coach's halftime speech was less a strategy talk than a stream of invective, hurling insults at every player who had missed a shot.

Invective is abusive, insulting language -- the coach isn't offering constructive criticism, just harsh verbal attacks.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

abuse: Abuse is the broadest word for cruel, insulting language -- any degrading talk counts, from a schoolyard taunt to a shouted slur. Invective is abuse with rhetorical force: sustained, pointed, often public attacking language, the kind that fills a furious review.

vituperation: Vituperation is bitter, sustained verbal abuse aimed at a person -- a stream of insults directed at someone in particular. Invective is broader in target: the same violent language can be turned on a person, a policy, or an idea. All vituperation is invective; not every burst of invective has a single victim.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

praise: words expressing approval

compliment: a polite expression of admiration

Where it sits · how harsh the words become — criticism → invective → tongue-lashing

criticism vs. invective: Criticism is far milder than invective -- it points out faults and can sting, but it stays reasoned argument. Invective abandons argument for attack: abusive, insulting language meant to wound.

tongue-lashing vs. invective: A tongue-lashing is even harsher than invective on the page -- the same abusive language, but delivered in person and at full volume, aimed straight at you for as long as the anger lasts.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: against, into (Latin)

root — vect

root — vect: carried (Latin vehere, 'to carry')

suffix — -ive

suffix — -ive: tending to, having the nature of (Latin -ivus)

Put it together

Put it together: Invective comes from Latin in- ('against') + vehere ('to carry') + -ivus -- literally 'carried against' someone, meaning language hurled at them as an attack.

Root Check

Word Choice

Invective is the abusive language itself -- the harsh words someone actually says or writes -- which makes it different from rancor (the underlying bitter feeling) and vilify (the act of using such language to damage someone's reputation).
